title: Exchange of contracts
subtitle: The point of no return, and the Law Society's Formulae for telephone exchange
objectives: Explain why exchange of contracts, not the signing of the contract, is the point at which a sale becomes binding and irrevocable
Identify the Law Society's Formulae A, B and C for exchanging contracts by telephone, fax or email, and select the correct formula for a given transaction structure
Apply the exchange process to a transaction in a chain and advise on the practical consequences of exchanging before a client is genuinely ready to complete

leadingAuthorities.role: A signed contract for the sale of land is not binding on either party until exchange takes place

leadingAuthorities.citation: Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s 2
leadingAuthorities.role: Formality requirement: a contract for the sale of land must be in writing, incorporate all agreed terms and be signed by or on behalf of each party
Used where one firm already holds both parts of the contract, signed by both clients
Used where each firm holds its own client's signed part; the standard bilateral exchange
Used to synchronise exchange across a chain of transactions, releasing each link only once every link is ready

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can state that 'exchange makes the contract binding' without hesitation. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the rule — this lesson is about running the exchange call itself, and knowing which formula protects your client when it goes wrong.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well here on recall before. The test pool is weighted towards applying the right formula to a fact pattern and spotting the practical trap in a chain — expect scenarios, not definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state, without prompting, why a signed contract is not yet a binding one. The rest of the lesson assumes that distinction is solid.

overview.hook: Both parties have signed. The price is agreed, the mortgage offer is in, the survey came back clean. And yet either side can still walk away with no legal consequence at all — because nothing has happened yet that the law calls binding. Then a solicitor picks up the phone, reads a fixed script to another solicitor, and in the space of about ninety seconds a sale that could have collapsed five minutes earlier becomes one that cannot lawfully be undone. That call is exchange of contracts, and it is the single most consequential moment in a conveyancing transaction.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The Law Society's Formulae are professional conduct guidance rather than statute and are periodically revised; solicitors should always check they are using the current edition, but the underlying mechanics described here — three formulae, telephone confirmation, a fixed release moment — have been stable for many years.

parts.heading: Why a signed contract still isn't a binding one
parts.voice: argumentative — states the counter-intuitive rule, then justifies it
body: By the time a residential or commercial sale reaches this stage, both clients have typically already signed their part of the contract. It feels finished. It is not. English law treats a contract for the sale of land as unformed — not merely unenforceable, but not yet in existence as a binding agreement — until the parties' solicitors exchange those signed parts.

This is deliberate, and it exists for a reason worth stating plainly: land transactions are large, slow-moving and full of people who need a genuine last chance to pull out without being sued for it. A buyer whose mortgage offer is withdrawn the day before exchange, or a seller who receives a better offer, can walk away at that point with no liability beyond wasted costs. Once exchange happens, that door closes for both of them simultaneously.

The formal requirement sits in section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989: a contract for the sale of land must be in writing, must contain all the terms the parties have expressly agreed, and must be signed by or on behalf of each party. In practice this is satisfied by each side signing an identical part and those parts then being exchanged — physically or, far more commonly today, by the solicitors confirming by telephone that a fixed and final exchange has taken place under one of three agreed formulae.

components.definition: The moment, not the signing that precedes it, at which a contract for the sale of land becomes binding on both parties — conventionally achieved today by solicitors confirming by telephone, under a Law Society Formula, that exchange has taken place.

interaction.prompt: Both parties have signed their part of the contract but the solicitors have not yet exchanged. Can the seller still accept a higher offer from someone else without being liable to the original buyer?
options: Yes — nothing is binding until exchange takes place
No — signature alone creates a binding contract
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Eccles v Bryant is the classic authority for exactly this: a signed contract is not a binding one until exchange.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — re-read the rule. Signature is a precondition for exchange, not a substitute for it; until exchange happens, either party can walk away.

parts.heading: Formula A: one firm holds both signed parts
parts.voice: structural — explains a narrow, less common route before the standard one
body: Formula A is used in a specific and relatively unusual situation: where one firm already has physical possession of both signed parts of the contract — typically because the buyer's solicitor has sent their client's signed part to the seller's solicitor in advance of exchange, to be held to that solicitor's order.

Under Formula A, the seller's solicitor (holding both parts) telephones the buyer's solicitor, confirms the agreed terms — the deposit, the completion date, the parts held — and both solicitors confirm exchange has taken place at that moment. The seller's solicitor then inserts the date on both parts and sends the buyer's part of the contract to the buyer's solicitor.

Because one firm is holding funds and documents belonging to the other side's client before exchange has completed, Formula A carries a higher trust burden. It tends to be used where the parties or their solicitors already have an established relationship, or where a short chain makes the simpler route practical.

components.label: Formula A checklist
points: One firm holds both signed parts of the contract
That firm telephones the other firm to confirm the deposit, completion date and documents held
Both solicitors confirm exchange takes place at that moment on the call
The holding firm dates both parts and forwards the other side's part to that firm

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you Formula A, rather than Formula B, is the correct route here.
interaction.scenarioText: The buyer's solicitor has already posted their client's signed contract to the seller's solicitor, to be held pending exchange. The seller's solicitor now holds both signed parts and is ready to call to fix a completion date.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — Formula A applies precisely because one firm has physical custody of both signed parts before the exchange call happens.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at which firm is holding what. Formula A is defined by one firm already holding both signed parts — that's the fact that distinguishes it from the far more common Formula B.

parts.heading: Formula B: the standard bilateral exchange
parts.voice: reference-style — walks through the call students will script and rehearse
body: Formula B is the everyday case: each firm holds its own client's signed part of the contract, and exchange happens by the two solicitors confirming, on a recorded or witnessed telephone call, that each will hold their own client's signed part to the order of the other firm from that moment.

The call itself follows a predictable structure, and SQE1 fact patterns test whether you know what has to be agreed before the words 'we are now exchanging' can safely be said: the agreed completion date, the deposit amount and how it is held (as stakeholder or agent), and confirmation that each firm genuinely holds a signed, matching part.

Once the call confirms exchange, each solicitor dates their own part of the contract with that date and sends it to the other firm, together with the deposit (from the buyer's solicitor) where that has not already been sent. From that second, both parties are bound.

components.label: Formula B: what must be agreed before the exchange words are said
points: The deposit amount and the capacity in which it is held (stakeholder or agent)
That each firm holds a signed part matching the other's in its terms
Any other outstanding terms specific to the transaction

interaction.prompt: Put these steps of a Formula B exchange call in the correct order.
items: Each solicitor confirms they hold their own client's signed, matching part
The completion date and deposit terms are confirmed on the call
Both solicitors use the agreed exchange words to confirm exchange has taken place
Each solicitor dates their part and sends it, with the deposit, to the other firm
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure examiners expect you to recognise: confirm what's held, confirm the terms, exchange, then complete the paperwork that follows from it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the exchange words come only after both the documents held and the key terms have been confirmed on the call, never before.

parts.heading: Formula C: exchanging inside a chain
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story of a chain to motivate the doctrine
body: Most residential sales in England and Wales sit inside a chain: a first-time buyer at one end, an onward purchase at the other, and several linked transactions in between, each dependent on the others exchanging on the same day. Formula B alone cannot manage this safely — if one link exchanges early and a later link falls through, that solicitor's client is bound to buy or sell a property that no longer connects to anything.

Formula C solves this by allowing a solicitor in the middle of a chain to exchange contracts on their own sale or purchase while releasing exchange only once every other link they depend on is also ready. In practice, each firm agrees a 'release time' by which every link must confirm readiness; when the last link confirms, a rapid sequence of Formula B-style calls exchanges every transaction in the chain within minutes of each other.

The critical discipline of Formula C is that a solicitor who has taken instructions to exchange 'subject to release' must not release their own link until they have genuine confirmation — not an assumption — that every other link is also ready. Releasing early defeats the entire purpose of using Formula C in the first place.

components.title: How a Formula C chain exchange runs
components.description: The sequence a solicitor manages when several linked transactions must exchange simultaneously.

nodes.label: Each firm in the chain confirms it is ready to exchange, subject to release
A release time is agreed by which every link must confirm readiness
At the release time, has every link in the chain confirmed?
Yes → each link exchanges in rapid succession, effectively simultaneously
No → no link releases; the release time is extended or the chain does not exchange that day

components.textAlternative: Each firm in the chain first confirms readiness subject to release, and a release time is agreed. If every link confirms by that time, every transaction exchanges in rapid succession. If any link has not confirmed, no link releases — the release time is extended or the chain does not exchange that day.

interaction.prompt: A solicitor acting for a seller in the middle of a five-link chain has confirmed readiness to exchange, subject to release. Two other links have not yet confirmed. What should the solicitor do?
options: Exchange immediately to avoid losing the sale
Wait — do not release exchange on this link until every link has confirmed readiness
Exchange only on the seller's own sale, leaving the linked purchase to exchange separately later
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The entire purpose of Formula C is to prevent exactly this risk — no link releases until every dependent link is genuinely ready.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reconsider what Formula C is for. Exchanging one link before the rest of the chain confirms readiness can leave a client bound to a transaction that no longer has a matching sale or purchase at the other end.

parts.heading: After exchange: what a client cannot undo
parts.voice: direct — sets out the consequences the tests will probe
body: Once exchange has taken place, both parties are contractually bound to complete on the agreed date. Risk in the property generally passes to the buyer from exchange (subject to the contract terms, which usually require the buyer to insure from that point), and the deposit — typically 10% — is at risk: if the buyer fails to complete without lawful excuse, the seller may in principle forfeit the deposit and seek damages or specific performance; if the seller fails to complete, the buyer has equivalent remedies.

This is why the most important practical advice in this lesson has nothing to do with the mechanics of the telephone call: a solicitor should never exchange contracts until the client is genuinely ready to be irrevocably bound — removal arranged, mortgage offer in place and not about to expire, and (in a chain) every dependent transaction accounted for. Clients under time pressure sometimes ask their solicitor to exchange 'to be safe' before these things are settled; that instinct is exactly backwards.

A solicitor who exchanges without clear client authority to do so, or before confirming the client can in fact complete on the agreed date, exposes the client to real financial and legal risk — and exposes themselves to a professional negligence claim if things go wrong.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that because exchange is the 'safe' irrevocable step, exchanging as early as possible protects the client.
components.whyItsWrong: Exchange protects a client from the other side walking away — but it also removes the client's own ability to walk away. Exchanging before a client can actually complete (funds, chain, removals) converts a flexible negotiation into a binding obligation the client may not be able to meet, with real financial consequences for failing to complete.

interaction.prompt: A buyer's mortgage offer expires in three weeks and removals are not yet booked. The buyer, anxious about losing the property, asks their solicitor to exchange contracts today with a completion date in six weeks. What is the solicitor's best next step?
options: Exchange immediately, since the buyer has given clear instructions
Advise the buyer of the risk of exchanging before completion arrangements and mortgage timing are secure, before proceeding
Refuse to exchange under any circumstances until removals are booked
interaction.trapExplanation: Following instructions immediately looks client-focused, but a solicitor's duty includes advising on the practical risk before acting on an instruction that could leave the client contractually bound but unable to complete — for example if the mortgage offer lapses before the completion date.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The client can still instruct the solicitor to proceed after being advised — but exchanging without flagging the mismatch between the mortgage offer's expiry and the completion date would be poor practice.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Think about what advice, not just action, the solicitor owes here. Client instructions are followed, but only once the client understands the risk of being bound before completion is actually achievable.

testPool.prompt: A seller and buyer have each signed identical parts of a contract for the sale of a house, but the solicitors have not yet spoken to confirm exchange. Is either party currently bound to the transaction?
options: No — signature alone does not create a binding contract for the sale of land
Yes — signing the contract is itself sufficient to bind both parties
Only the seller is bound, not the buyer
Only the buyer is bound, not the seller
testPool.explanation: Eccles v Bryant confirms that a signed contract for the sale of land is not binding until exchange. Before that point either party may withdraw without breaching a contract, though they may still lose wasted costs.

testPool.prompt: Which formula is used where one firm already holds both parties' signed parts of the contract before the exchange call takes place?
options: Formula A
Formula B
Formula C
There is no formula for this situation
testPool.explanation: Formula A applies specifically where one firm has physical custody of both signed parts, typically because the other firm has already sent its client's signed part across in advance.

testPool.prompt: Which formula is specifically designed to synchronise exchange across several linked transactions in a chain?
options: Formula A
Formula B
Formula C
Formula D
testPool.explanation: Formula C introduces a release mechanism so that no link in a chain exchanges until every dependent link has confirmed it is ready, avoiding one client being bound to a transaction that no longer connects to the rest of the chain.

testPool.prompt: Under a standard Formula B exchange, which two commercial terms must the solicitors confirm on the call before using the words that exchange contracts?
options: The completion date and the deposit amount and capacity in which it is held
The buyer's mortgage lender and the seller's estate agent
The property's council tax band and its EPC rating
The buyer's solicitor's professional indemnity insurer
testPool.explanation: The completion date and the deposit terms (amount, and whether held as stakeholder or agent) are the essential commercial terms that must be confirmed as matching before the exchange words are used.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's solicitor argues that because their client has signed the contract and paid a holding deposit to the estate agent, the seller cannot now accept a higher offer. Is this correct?
options: Yes, because payment of any deposit always creates a binding obligation
No, because a holding deposit paid to an estate agent before exchange does not create a binding contract; only exchange does
Yes, because signing the contract alone is sufficient once a deposit has changed hands
No, because only a deposit paid directly to the seller's solicitor can ever bind the parties
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think any deposit payment locks in the deal, but an estate agent's holding deposit is a separate, informal arrangement with no bearing on the formal exchange requirement — the seller remains free to accept another offer, however unwelcome that is to the disappointed buyer.
testPool.explanation: Nothing short of exchange itself (or, exceptionally, a collateral contract deliberately created) binds either party in a land sale; a holding deposit to an agent is not exchange.

testPool.prompt: A trainee assumes Formula A is the 'default' formula because it comes first alphabetically, and plans to use it for a straightforward two-party sale where each firm holds its own client's signed part. Is this the correct formula?
options: Yes, Formula A is always the default starting point
No — Formula B applies where each firm holds its own client's signed part; Formula A requires one firm to hold both
No — Formula C should be used for any two-party sale
Yes, provided both solicitors agree in advance
testPool.trapExplanation: The letters A, B and C do not indicate a hierarchy of preference — each formula answers to a different factual situation, and using the wrong one because it 'sounds standard' misstates which firm is holding which documents.
testPool.explanation: Formula B, not A, is the standard bilateral formula used where each firm retains custody of its own client's signed part until the exchange call.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor in a four-link chain has agreed a release time of 3pm. At 2.55pm, three of the four links have confirmed readiness; the fourth has gone silent. The solicitor's client is anxious and asks them to exchange anyway on the assumption the fourth link will confirm shortly. What should the solicitor do?
options: Exchange at 3pm as agreed, since three of the four links are ready
Do not release exchange on any link until the fourth link has actually confirmed, regardless of the agreed release time
Exchange only the client's own sale, leaving the related purchase unresolved
Extend the client's mortgage offer before deciding what to do
testPool.trapExplanation: Treating the release time as a deadline that triggers exchange regardless of confirmation defeats the purpose of Formula C — the release time is when confirmation is due, not a substitute for it if confirmation has not actually arrived.
testPool.explanation: The safeguard in Formula C is real confirmation from every link, not an assumption based on how many links have already replied or how close the agreed time is.

testPool.prompt: A seller's solicitor is holding both parties' signed contracts, the buyer's part having been sent over the previous week. The two solicitors are now ready to speak and fix a completion date. Which formula applies?
options: Formula A
Formula B
Formula C
No formula is needed because the contract is already exchanged
testPool.explanation: Because one firm already holds both signed parts, this is a Formula A exchange — the holding firm confirms terms with the other firm and dates both parts once exchange is confirmed.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's solicitor exchanges contracts on instructions from the client, without first checking whether the client's mortgage offer will still be valid on the agreed completion date six weeks later. The offer lapses before completion, and the buyer cannot complete. What has most likely gone wrong from a professional practice standpoint?
options: Nothing — the solicitor correctly followed the client's clear instruction to exchange
The solicitor should have advised on the risk of exchanging before confirming completion could realistically be achieved on the agreed date
The seller's solicitor is solely responsible because they set the completion date
The mortgage lender is responsible because it set the expiry date on the offer
testPool.explanation: A solicitor's duty is not simply to act on instructions but to advise on foreseeable risk before doing something irrevocable — exchanging without checking mortgage timing against the completion date is the practical trap this lesson exists to flag.

testPool.prompt: Immediately after a Formula B exchange call, which party's solicitor is expected to send the deposit to the other firm, if it has not already been transferred?
options: The buyer's solicitor sends the deposit to the seller's solicitor
The seller's solicitor sends the deposit to the buyer's solicitor
Neither — the deposit is paid directly by the buyer to the seller
The estate agent transfers the deposit to the seller's solicitor
testPool.explanation: The buyer's solicitor sends the deposit (commonly 10% of the price) to the seller's solicitor once exchange is confirmed, alongside dating and forwarding the buyer's part of the contract.

testPool.prompt: After exchange, a fire damages the property before completion and the buyer has not yet arranged insurance. Which statement best reflects the usual position under a standard contract?
options: Risk generally passes to the buyer from exchange, so the buyer is usually expected to have insured from that point
Risk never passes to the buyer until completion, so the seller bears any loss regardless of insurance arrangements
Risk is irrelevant because insurers always cover the property regardless of who holds the policy
The transaction is automatically void once any damage occurs after exchange
testPool.explanation: Under most standard contract terms, risk passes to the buyer at exchange, which is exactly why solicitors advise buyers to have insurance in place from exchange, not from completion.

testPool.prompt: Under section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, which of the following is NOT a requirement for a valid contract for the sale of land?
options: The contract must be in writing
The contract must incorporate all the terms the parties have expressly agreed
The contract must be signed by or on behalf of each party
The contract must be witnessed by an independent solicitor
testPool.explanation: Section 2 requires writing, inclusion of all express terms, and signature by or on behalf of each party. It does not require independent witnessing — that formality applies to deeds, not to the underlying contract.

testPool.prompt: A contract for the sale of land is agreed orally over the telephone, with no written document at all. Applying section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, is this a valid contract for the sale of land?
options: Yes — an oral agreement on clear terms is sufficient for land
No — section 2 requires the contract to be in writing and signed; an oral agreement alone does not satisfy this
Yes, provided the price is agreed and a deposit is paid
No, unless the transaction value is below a statutory threshold
testPool.explanation: Section 2 is a formality requirement, not merely evidential — without a written, signed document incorporating the terms, there is no valid contract for the sale of land at all, whatever was said on the phone.

testPool.prompt: Two parties sign separate letters that between them contain all the agreed terms of a land sale, each letter signed by only one party and exchanged between them. Does this satisfy section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989?
options: No — section 2 requires a single document signed by both parties, with no exceptions
Yes — section 2 expressly permits the terms to be contained in a document signed by each party, where the documents are exchanged
No — only a deed can satisfy the formality requirement for land contracts
Yes, but only if a solicitor countersigns both letters
testPool.explanation: Section 2 allows for the terms to be set out in each part and signed by one party, the two parts then being exchanged — this is precisely the structure that the exchange of contracts practice is built around.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating exchange as purely procedural — a call to make once the paperwork is ready — rather than as the moment a client loses the ability to walk away. The safest answer to 'should we exchange now?' is never automatic; it depends on whether the client can actually complete on the date being fixed.
